title: Some Questions We Know to Ask
short: Some Questions We Know to Ask
lead: Physics has open questions at every scale. This section gathers a sample of those physicists now know to ask, on the largest scale of galaxies and the universe, on the intermediate scale of the matter around us, and on the smallest scale of particles and forces.
objectives: Identify sample questions to be asked on the largest scales.
Identify sample questions to be asked on the intermediate scale.
Identify sample questions to be asked on the smallest scales.
summary_html:
• On the largest scale, the questions which can be asked may be about dark matter, dark energy, black holes, quasars, and other aspects of the universe.
  • On the intermediate scale, we can query about gravity, phase transitions, nonlinear phenomena, high-$\kTempc$ superconductors, and magnetic effects on materials.
  • On the smallest scale, questions may be about quarks and leptons, fundamental forces, stability of protons, and existence of monopoles.
notes: Nothing of the module is left out. The first question on the largest scale keeps the book's “just barely closed” as printed, where Dark Matter and Closure says the universe should be just barely open.

exercises.prompt: For experimental evidence, particularly of previously unobserved phenomena, to be taken seriously it must be reproducible or of sufficiently high quality that a single observation is meaningful. Supernova 1987A is not reproducible. How do we know observations of it were valid? The fifth force is not broadly accepted. Is this due to lack of reproducibility or poor-quality experiments (or both)? Discuss why forefront experiments are more subject to observational problems than those involving established phenomena.

answer.solution: Supernova 1987A could not be repeated, but it was observed by many independent instruments at once: telescopes around the world recorded its light, and neutrino detectors on different continents recorded a burst of neutrinos arriving within seconds of one another. Independent observations that agree with each other, and with what is expected of a collapsing stellar core, make a single event meaningful. The fifth force fails on reproducibility above all: the claimed effects have not been detected consistently by other groups. The proposed forces have strengths similar to gravity, so each experiment must pick a tiny effect out of much larger ones, where a small systematic error can look like a signal; the quality of the measurements is therefore also at issue. Forefront experiments look for effects no one has yet seen, so the signal is near the limit of what the instruments can detect, the apparatus is often new, the events may be rare or unrepeatable, and there is no accepted result to compare against that would expose an error. Established phenomena have been measured many times by many methods, and a faulty measurement stands out against the rest.

exercises.prompt: Discuss whether you think there are limits to what humans can understand about the laws of physics. Support your arguments.

answer.solution: Either position can be argued; what matters is the support. For limits: some questions may lie beyond experiment, as superstrings would be 17 orders of magnitude smaller than the smallest details yet observed, and the energies at which the forces are thought to unify may never be reached in an accelerator; experiment may only ever show that the proton is very long lived, never that it is stable; and quantum mechanics and relativity already describe a world far from everyday intuition. Against limits: physics has repeatedly answered questions once thought unanswerable, often indirectly, as the early universe is studied through particle accelerators and the cosmic microwave background, and mathematics describes what cannot be pictured. A careful answer may separate what can be tested from what can be understood, and note, as the section does, that each answer raises new questions, so there always seems to be more to know.
